**Lugano** (/luːˈɡɑːnoʊ/,[[5]](Lugano#cite_note-5)[[6]](Lugano#cite_note-6)[[7]](Lugano#cite_note-7) [UK](British_English "British English") also /lʊˈɡænoʊ/,[[8]](Lugano#cite_note-8) Italian: [luˈɡaːno]; [Ticinese](Ticinese_dialect "Ticinese dialect"): *Lugan* [lyˈɡãː]) is a [city](City "City") and municipality in <Switzerland>, part of the [Lugano District](Lugano_District "Lugano District") in the canton of <Ticino>. It is the largest city of both Ticino and the Italian-speaking southern Switzerland. Lugano has a population (as of December 2020) of 62,315,[[9]](Lugano#cite_note-Stat2020_TI-9) and an [urban agglomeration](Urban_agglomeration "Urban agglomeration") of over 150,000. It is the [ninth largest Swiss city](List_of_cities_in_Switzerland "List of cities in Switzerland").

The city lies on [Lake Lugano](Lake_Lugano "Lake Lugano"), at its largest width, and, together with the adjacent town of [Paradiso](Paradiso%2C_Switzerland "Paradiso, Switzerland"), occupies the entire bay of Lugano. The territory of the municipality encompasses a much larger region on both sides of the lake, with numerous isolated villages. The region of Lugano is surrounded by the [Lugano Prealps](Lugano_Prealps "Lugano Prealps"), the latter extending on most of the <Sottoceneri> region, the southernmost part of Ticino and Switzerland. Both western and eastern parts of the municipality share an international border with Italy.

Described as a market town since 984, Lugano was the object of continuous disputes between the sovereigns of <Como> and <Milan>[until it became part](Transalpine_campaigns_of_the_Old_Swiss_Confederacy "Transalpine campaigns of the Old Swiss Confederacy") of the [Old Swiss Confederation](Old_Swiss_Confederation "Old Swiss Confederation") in 1513. In 1803, the political municipality of Lugano was created, following the establishment of the canton. Since 1882, Lugano is an important stop on the international [Gotthard Railway](Gotthard_Railway "Gotthard Railway"). The rail brought a decisive contribution to the development of tourism and more generally of the tertiary sector which are, to this day, predominant in the economy of the city.

In 1956, Lugano hosted the first ever Eurovision Song Contest.

## Name and coat of arms

The toponym is first recorded in 804, in the form *Luanasco*, in 874 as *Luano*, and from 1189 as *Lugano*. German-language variants of the name (now no longer in use) were *Lowens*, *Lauis*, *Lauwis*, *Louwerz*.[[10]](Lugano#cite_note-City_History-10)[[11]](Lugano#cite_note-HDS_Commune-11) The local [Lombard](Lombard_language "Lombard language") form of the name is rendered *Lugan*.[[12]](Lugano#cite_note-12) The etymology of the name is uncertain, suggestions include derivation from [Latin](Latin_language "Latin language") *lucus* ("grove"),[[13]](Lugano#cite_note-13) from a vulgar Latin *lakvannus* ("lake-dweller")[[14]](Lugano#cite_note-14) and from the god <Lugus>.[[15]](Lugano#cite_note-15)

### Pre-history

The shores of Lake Lugano have been inhabited since the [Stone Age](Stone_Age "Stone Age"). Within the modern city limits (Breganzona, [Castagnola](Castagnola%2C_Switzerland "Castagnola, Switzerland"), Davesco and Gandria) a number of [ground stones](Ground_stone "Ground stone") or [quern-stones](Quern-stone "Quern-stone") have been found. In the area surrounding Lugano, items from the [Copper Age](Copper_Age "Copper Age") and the [Iron Age](Iron_Age "Iron Age") have been found.[[16]](Lugano#cite_note-HDS_Prehistory-16) There are [Etruscan](Etruscan_language "Etruscan language") monuments at Davesco-Soragno (5th to 2nd century BC), Pregassona (3rd to 2nd century BC), and Viganello (3rd to 2nd century BC). Graves with jewelry and household items have been found in Aldesago, Davesco, Pazzallo and Pregassona along with [Celtic](Celts "Celts") money in Viganello.

The region around Lake Lugano was settled by the [Romans](Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") by the 1st century BC. There was an important Roman town north of Lugano at <Bioggio>.[[16]](Lugano#cite_note-HDS_Prehistory-16) There are fewer traces of the Romans in Lugano, but several inscriptions, graves and coins indicate that some Romans lived in what would become Lugano.

With over 110,000 residents it is the country's [sixth-largest city by population](List_of_cities_in_Switzerland "List of cities in Switzerland"), and is the ninth-largest agglomeration with about 140,000 inhabitants.[[3]](Winterthur#cite_note-3) Located about 20 kilometres (12 mi) northeast of [Zürich](Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich"), Winterthur is a service and high-tech industrial [satellite city](Satellite_city "Satellite city") within [Greater Zürich](Greater_Z%C3%BCrich "Greater Zürich").

The official language of Winterthur is German,[[note 1]](Winterthur#cite_note-4) but the main spoken language is the local variant of the [Alemannic](Alemannic_German "Alemannic German") [Swiss German](Swiss_German "Swiss German") dialect, [Zürich German](Z%C3%BCrich_German "Zürich German"). Winterthur is usually abbreviated as *Winti* in the local dialect and by its inhabitants.

Winterthur is connected to Germany by direct trains and has links to [Zurich Airport](Zurich_Airport "Zurich Airport"). It is also a regional transport hub: the A1 motorway from <Geneva> through to [St. Margrethen](St._Margrethen "St. Margrethen") connects in Winterthur with the A4 motorway heading north toward <Schaffhausen> and the A7 motorway heading close to the Swiss-German border at <Kreuzlingen>. There are also roads leading to other places such as <Turbenthal>. The [railway station](Winterthur_railway_station "Winterthur railway station") is the fourth busiest railway station in Switzerland,[[4]](Winterthur#cite_note-5) and is 20 minutes away by train from Zürich.

## History

*<Vitudurum>* was a *[vicus](Vicus_(Rome) "Vicus (Rome)")* in what is now <Oberwinterthur> during the [Roman era](Switzerland_in_the_Roman_era "Switzerland in the Roman era") (first century BC to third century AD). It was fortified into a *[castrum](Castrum "Castrum")* at the end of the third century, apparently in reaction to the incipient [Alamannic invasion](Alemanni#Conflicts_with_the_Roman_Empire "Alemanni").

There was an [Alamannic](Alamanni "Alamanni") settlement on the site in the seventh century.

In a [battle near Winterthur](Battle_of_Winterthur_(919) "Battle of Winterthur (919)") in 919, [Burchard II of Swabia](Burchard_II%2C_Duke_of_Swabia "Burchard II, Duke of Swabia") asserted his control over the [Thurgau](Turgowe "Turgowe") within the [Duchy of Swabia](Duchy_of_Swabia "Duchy of Swabia") against the claims of [Rudolph II of Burgundy](Rudolph_II_of_Burgundy "Rudolph II of Burgundy").

The [counts of Winterthur](Counts_of_Winterthur "Counts of Winterthur"), a cadet branch of the family of the [counts of Bregenz](Counts_of_Bregenz "Counts of Bregenz"), built [Kyburg castle](Kyburg_castle "Kyburg castle") in the tenth century. With the extinction of the counts of Winterthur in 1053, the castle passed to the [counts of Dillingen](Counts_of_Dillingen "Counts of Dillingen"). **Basel** (/ˈbɑːzəl/ *BAH-zəl*, German: [ˈbaːzl̩] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/a/a9/De-Basel.ogg/De-Basel.ogg.mp3)ⓘ), also known as **Basle** (/bɑːl/ *BAHL*),[[note 1]](Basel#cite_note-4) is a city in northwestern <Switzerland> on the river [Rhine](High_Rhine "High Rhine").[[4]](Basel#cite_note-5) Basel is Switzerland's [third-most-populous](List_of_cities_in_Switzerland "List of cities in Switzerland") city (after [Zürich](Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich") and <Geneva>), with 177,595 inhabitants within the city municipality limits.[[5]](Basel#cite_note-6) The official language of Basel is (the Swiss variety of Standard) [German](Swiss_Standard_German "Swiss Standard German"), and the main spoken language is the local [Basel German](Basel_German "Basel German") dialect.[[6]](Basel#cite_note-7)

Basel is commonly considered to be the cultural capital of Switzerland[[7]](Basel#cite_note-8)[[8]](Basel#cite_note-9) and the city is famous for its many [museums](Museums_in_Basel "Museums in Basel"), including the [Kunstmuseum](Kunstmuseum_Basel "Kunstmuseum Basel"), which is the first collection of art accessible to the public in the world (1661) and the largest museum of [art in Switzerland](Swiss_art "Swiss art"), the [Fondation Beyeler](Fondation_Beyeler "Fondation Beyeler") (located in <Riehen>), the [Museum Tinguely](Museum_Tinguely "Museum Tinguely") and the [Museum of Contemporary Art](Museum_of_Contemporary_Art_(Basel) "Museum of Contemporary Art (Basel)"), which is the first public museum of contemporary art in Europe.[[9]](Basel#cite_note-10) Forty museums are spread throughout the city-canton, making Basel one of the largest cultural centres in relation to its size and population in Europe.[[10]](Basel#cite_note-11)

The [University of Basel](University_of_Basel "University of Basel"), Switzerland's oldest university (founded in 1460),[[11]](Basel#cite_note-12) and the city's centuries-long commitment to [humanism](Humanism "Humanism"), have made Basel a safe haven at times of political unrest in other parts of Europe for such notable people as [Erasmus of Rotterdam](Erasmus_of_Rotterdam "Erasmus of Rotterdam"),[[12]](Basel#cite_note-13) the [Holbein](Hans_Holbein_the_Younger "Hans Holbein the Younger") family, [Friedrich Nietzsche](Friedrich_Nietzsche "Friedrich Nietzsche"),[[13]](Basel#cite_note-14) [Carl Jung](Carl_Jung "Carl Jung"), and in the 20th century also [Hermann Hesse](Hermann_Hesse "Hermann Hesse")[[14]](Basel#cite_note-15) and [Karl Jaspers](Karl_Jaspers "Karl Jaspers").[[15]](Basel#cite_note-16)

Basel was the seat of a [Prince-Bishopric](Prince-Bishopric_of_Basel "Prince-Bishopric of Basel") starting in the 11th century, and joined the [Swiss Confederacy](Old_Swiss_Confederacy "Old Swiss Confederacy") in 1501.[[16]](Basel#cite_note-17) The city has been a commercial hub and an important cultural centre since the <Renaissance>,[[17]](Basel#cite_note-18) and has emerged as a centre for the [chemical](Chemical_industry "Chemical industry") and [pharmaceutical industries](Pharmaceutical_industry "Pharmaceutical industry") in the 20th century.[[18]](Basel#cite_note-19) In 1897, Basel was chosen by [Theodor Herzl](Theodor_Herzl "Theodor Herzl") as the location for the first [World Zionist Congress](World_Zionist_Congress "World Zionist Congress"), and altogether the congress was held there ten times over a time span of 50 years, more than in any other location.[[19]](Basel#cite_note-20) The city is also home to the world headquarters of the [Bank for International Settlements](Bank_for_International_Settlements "Bank for International Settlements").[[20]](Basel#cite_note-21) The name of the city is internationally known through institutions like the [Basel Accords](Basel_Accords "Basel Accords"),[[21]](Basel#cite_note-22) [Art Basel](Art_Basel "Art Basel")[[22]](Basel#cite_note-23) and [FC Basel](FC_Basel "FC Basel").[[23]](Basel#cite_note-24)

In 2019 Basel was ranked the tenth most liveable city in the world by [Mercer](Mercer_(consulting_firm) "Mercer (consulting firm)").[[24]](Basel#cite_note-25)

## Name

The name of Basel is first recorded as *Basilia* in the 3rd century (237/8), at the time referring to the [Roman castle](Basel_oppidum "Basel oppidum"). This name is mostly interpreted as deriving from the personal name *Basilius*, from a toponym *villa Basilia* ("[estate](Roman_villa "Roman villa") of Basilius") or similar.[[25]](Basel#cite_note-26)

Another suggestion derives it from a name *Basilia* attested in northern France as a development of *basilica*, the term for a public or church building (as in <Bazeilles>), but all of these names reference early church buildings of the 4th or 5th century and cannot be adduced for the 3rd-century attestation of *Basilia*.[[26]](Basel#cite_note-27)[[27]](Basel#cite_note-Kristol-28)

By popular etymology, or simple assonance, the [basilisk](Basilisk "Basilisk") becomes closely associated with the city, used as [heraldic supporter](Heraldic_supporter "Heraldic supporter") from 1448, represented on coins minted by the city, and frequently found in ornaments.

The [Middle French](Middle_French "Middle French") form *Basle* was adopted into English, but this form has fallen gradually out of use although it continues to be used in some sections of [British English](British_English "British English") including the <BBC>.[[28]](Basel#cite_note-29) [[29]](Basel#cite_note-30) Currently, the spelling *Basel* is most often used, to match the official German spelling. In French *Basle* was still in use in the 18th century, but was gradually replaced by the modern French spelling *Bâle*. **Bern** ( Swiss Standard German: [bɛrn] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/1/1d/De-Bern.ogg/De-Bern.ogg.mp3)ⓘ) or **Berne** (French: [bɛʁn] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/f/f2/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-DSwissK-Berne.wav/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-DSwissK-Berne.wav.mp3)ⓘ)[[note 1]](Bern#cite_note-3) is the *[de facto](De_facto "De facto")* [capital](Capital_city "Capital city") of <Switzerland>, referred to as the "[federal city](Federal_city "Federal city")".[[note 2]](Bern#cite_note-4)[[3]](Bern#cite_note-deFacto-5) With a population of about 133,000 (as of 2022), Bern is the [fifth-most populous city](List_of_cities_in_Switzerland "List of cities in Switzerland") in Switzerland, behind [Zürich](Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich"), <Geneva>, <Basel> and <Lausanne>.[[4]](Bern#cite_note-StatBern-6) The Bern agglomeration, which includes 36 municipalities, had a population of 406,900 in 2014.[[5]](Bern#cite_note-Agglomeration-7) The [metropolitan area](Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") had a population of 660,000 in 2000.[[6]](Bern#cite_note-8)

Bern is also the capital of the [canton of Bern](Canton_of_Bern "Canton of Bern"), the second-most populous of [Switzerland's cantons](Cantons_of_Switzerland "Cantons of Switzerland"). The official language is [German](German_language "German language"),[[note 3]](Bern#cite_note-9) but the main spoken language is the local variant of the [Alemannic](Alemannic_German "Alemannic German") [Swiss German](Swiss_German "Swiss German") dialect, [Bernese German](Bernese_German "Bernese German"). In 1983, the [historic old town](Old_City_of_Bern "Old City of Bern") (in [German](German_language "German language"): *Altstadt*) in the centre of Bern became a <UNESCO> [World Heritage Site](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[7]](Bern#cite_note-10) It is notably surrounded by the <Aare>, a major river of the [Swiss Plateau](Swiss_Plateau "Swiss Plateau").

Although fortified settlements were established since antiquity, the medieval city proper was founded by the [Zähringer](Z%C3%A4hringer "Zähringer") ruling family, probably in 1191 by [Berthold V, Duke of Zähringen](Berthold_V%2C_Duke_of_Z%C3%A4hringen "Berthold V, Duke of Zähringen"). Bern was made a [free imperial city](Free_imperial_city "Free imperial city") in 1218 and, in 1353, it joined the [Swiss Confederacy](Old_Swiss_Confederacy "Old Swiss Confederacy"), becoming one of its eight early cantons. Since then, Bern became a large [city-state](City-state "City-state") and a prominent actor of Swiss history by pursuing a policy of sovereign territorial expansion. Since the 15th century, the city was progressively rebuilt and acquired its current characteristics. Bern was made the Federal City in 1848. From about 5,000 inhabitants in the 15th century, the city passed the 100,000 mark in the 1920s.

## Etymology

See also [Other names of Bern](Names_of_European_cities_in_different_languages%3A_B "Names of European cities in different languages: B")

The etymology of the name "Bern" is uncertain. According to the local legend, based on [folk etymology](Folk_etymology "Folk etymology"), [Berchtold V, Duke of Zähringen](Berthold_V%2C_Duke_of_Z%C3%A4hringen "Berthold V, Duke of Zähringen"), the founder of the city of Bern, vowed to name the city after the first animal he met on the hunt, and this turned out to be a bear. It has long been considered likely that the city was named after the Italian city of <Verona>, which at the time was known as *Bern* in [Middle High German](Middle_High_German "Middle High German"). The city was sometimes referred to as *Bern im [Üechtland](%C3%9Cechtland "Üechtland")* to distinguish it from Verona.[[8]](Bern#cite_note-11) As a result of the finding of the [Bern zinc tablet](Bern_zinc_tablet "Bern zinc tablet") in the 1980s, it is now more common to assume that the city was named after a pre-existing toponym of Celtic origin, possibly **berna* "cleft".[[9]](Bern#cite_note-12) The bear was the heraldic animal of the [seal and coat of arms of Bern](Coat_of_arms_of_Bern "Coat of arms of Bern") from at least the 1220s. The earliest reference to the keeping of live bears in the *[Bärengraben](B%C3%A4rengraben "Bärengraben")* dates to the 1440s.

## History

Main article: [History of Bern](History_of_Bern "History of Bern")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Bern](Timeline_of_Bern "Timeline of Bern").

### Early history

No [archaeological](Archaeological "Archaeological") evidence that indicates a settlement on the site of today's city centre prior to the 12th century has been found so far.
